name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_MCQ_Q01 - Industrial and laboratory preparation methods of phenols

questiontext.text:
Given below are four statements regarding the methods of preparation of phenol:

Statement I: Commercial production of phenol from cumene involves oxidation of cumene with air to cumene hydroperoxide, which upon treatment with dilute acid yields phenol along with acetone as an important by-product.

Statement II: In the industrial Dow process, chlorobenzene is hydrolyzed to sodium phenoxide by heating with molten sodium hydroxide at \(623\text{ K}\) and \(300\text{ atm}\) pressure, which on acidification yields phenol.

Statement III: Benzene on treatment with oleum gives benzene sulphonic acid, which upon heating with molten sodium hydroxide followed by acidification of the resulting sodium phenoxide produces phenol.

Statement IV: Aniline is diazotized by nitrous acid at \(273\text{--}278\text{ K}\) to benzene diazonium chloride, which upon warming with water hydrolyzes with the liberation of nitrogen gas to produce chlorobenzene.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of cumene oxidation and acid cleavage
Cumene (isopropylbenzene) undergoes aerial oxidation in the presence of atmospheric oxygen to form cumene hydroperoxide. Subsequent treatment of cumene hydroperoxide with dilute mineral acid (\(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)) induces a rearrangement and cleavage reaction yielding phenol and propan-2-one (acetone). Since acetone is obtained in substantial quantities as a commercially valuable co-product, this route constitutes the predominant industrial method for synthesizing phenol. Thus, the assertion regarding the conversion of cumene to phenol and acetone through cumene hydroperoxide intermediate is scientifically accurate.

Step 2: Evaluation of Dow's process from chlorobenzene
Chlorobenzene exhibits low reactivity towards nucleophilic substitution under ambient conditions due to resonance stabilization of the carbon-chlorine bond, \(\text{sp}^2\)-hybridization of the aromatic carbon, and electronic repulsion. Consequently, conversion of chlorobenzene into sodium phenoxide necessitates drastic reaction conditions: heating with aqueous or molten sodium hydroxide at \(623\text{ K}\) and an elevated pressure of \(300\text{ atm}\). Subsequent acidification of the sodium phenoxide intermediate with dilute hydrochloric acid furnishes free phenol. Hence, the description of Dow's process conditions and outcome is scientifically accurate.

Step 3: Evaluation of benzene sulphonation and alkali fusion
Benzene undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution when treated with oleum (fuming sulphuric acid, \(\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7\)) to form benzene sulphonic acid (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_3\text{H}\)). Fusing benzene sulphonic acid with molten sodium hydroxide at approximately \(573\text{--}623\text{ K}\) converts the sulphonic group into sodium phenoxide (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa}\)) with loss of sodium sulphite. Acidification of this sodium phenoxide mixture yields phenol. Therefore, the pathway converting benzene to phenol via benzene sulphonic acid and alkali fusion is scientifically accurate.

Step 4: Evaluation of diazonium salt hydrolysis
Primary aromatic amines such as aniline undergo diazotization upon treatment with nitrous acid (\(\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}\)) at low temperatures (\(273\text{--}278\text{ K}\)), generating benzene diazonium chloride (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-\)). When an aqueous solution of benzene diazonium chloride is warmed with water or treated with dilute acid, the diazonium group undergoes nucleophilic displacement by water with the evolution of nitrogen gas (\(\text{N}_2\)) and formation of hydrochloric acid, producing phenol (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}\)), not chlorobenzene (which would instead be formed by the Sandmeyer reaction using cuprous chloride, \(\text{Cu}_2\text{Cl}_2/\text{HCl}\)). Thus, the assertion that warming the diazonium salt with water forms chlorobenzene is incorrect.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Comparing the four evaluations confirms that the first, second, and third statements correctly describe the respective synthetic transformations, whereas the fourth statement misidentifies the hydrolysis product of benzene diazonium chloride as chlorobenzene rather than phenol.
Final Answer: Statements I, II and III only.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_MCQ_Q02 - Structural characteristics mechanism of cleavage and aromatic reactivity of ethers

questiontext.text:
Given below are four statements regarding the structure, preparation, and chemical reactions of ethers:

Statement I: In dialkyl ethers, the \(\text{C–O–C}\) bond angle is slightly greater than the normal tetrahedral angle of \(109.5^\circ\) due to repulsive steric interactions between the two bulky alkyl groups.

Statement II: Acid-catalysed dehydration of tertiary alcohols at \(413\text{ K}\) in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid gives symmetrical di-tert-alkyl ethers as the predominant product via an \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) pathway.

Statement III: Cleavage of tert-butyl methyl ether with an equimolar amount of hydroiodic acid at room temperature proceeds predominantly via an \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) pathway to yield tert-butyl iodide and methanol.

Statement IV: In electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions, the methoxy group (\(–\text{OCH}_3\)) attached to the benzene ring in anisole deactivates the aromatic nucleus towards incoming electrophiles while directing substitution to the ortho and para positions.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the bond angle in ethers
In ether molecules such as methoxymethane (\(\text{CH}_3–\text{O}–\text{CH}_3\)), the central oxygen atom is \(\text{sp}^3\)-hybridized and possesses two bonding electron pairs and two lone pairs. Although lone pair-lone pair repulsions tend to decrease bond angles below the standard tetrahedral angle of \(109^\circ28'\) (as observed in water where the \(\text{H–O–H}\) bond angle is \(104.5^\circ\)), the presence of bulky alkyl substituents generates substantial repulsive steric interactions between the alkyl groups. This steric crowding overcomes the lone pair compression and opens the \(\text{C–O–C}\) bond angle to approximately \(111.7^\circ\), which is larger than the ideal tetrahedral angle. Therefore, the assertion regarding the ether bond angle and steric repulsions is scientifically accurate.

Step 2: Evaluation of dehydration of tertiary alcohols
Acid-catalysed dehydration of primary alcohols (such as ethanol) in concentrated \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) at \(413\text{ K}\) yields symmetrical ethers via a bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\text{S}_\text{N}2\)) mechanism. However, for secondary and tertiary alcohols, steric hindrance suppresses nucleophilic attack by another alcohol molecule on the protonated alcohol. Instead, tertiary alcohols rapidly form stable tertiary carbocations that undergo preferential elimination (E1 pathway) by loss of a \(\beta\)-proton to yield alkenes (such as 2-methylpropene) rather than di-tert-alkyl ethers. Thus, the statement claiming quantitative or predominant synthesis of di-tert-alkyl ethers from tertiary alcohols via dehydration is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of ether cleavage with hydroiodic acid
When an ether containing one primary alkyl group and one tertiary alkyl group (such as tert-butyl methyl ether) is cleaved with hydrogen iodide, the ether oxygen is initially protonated to form an oxonium ion. Because a relatively stable tertiary carbocation (\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+\)) can be formed readily upon departure of the neutral leaving group (\(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\)), the reaction proceeds predominantly through a unimolecular \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) mechanism rather than an \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) pathway. The nucleophilic iodide ion (\(\text{I}^-\)) subsequently captures the stable tert-butyl carbocation to form tert-butyl iodide, leaving methanol intact. Consequently, the assertion regarding the \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) mechanism and products is scientifically accurate.

Step 4: Evaluation of the electronic effect of the methoxy group in anisole
The methoxy group (\(–\text{OCH}_3\)) in anisole has an oxygen atom with lone pairs directly bonded to the \(\text{sp}^2\)-carbon of the aromatic ring. Although oxygen exerts an electron-withdrawing inductive effect (\(–\text{I}\)) due to its electronegativity, its stronger electron-donating resonance effect (\(+\text{R}\)) delocalizes lone-pair electron density into the ring, significantly enhancing electron density at the ortho and para positions. As a result, the methoxy group strongly activates the benzene ring towards electrophilic aromatic substitution (the rate of halogenation or nitration is substantially higher than that of benzene itself, allowing bromination without a Lewis acid catalyst). Thus, characterizing the methoxy group in anisole as deactivating is incorrect.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Review of the four evaluations confirms that the first and third statements are scientifically correct, whereas the second statement (incorrectly claiming ether formation from tertiary alcohols) and the fourth statement (incorrectly claiming the methoxy group is ring-deactivating) are incorrect.
Final Answer: Statements I and III only.
